## What the program does
Write class Logger that holds a list of Consumer<String> handlers and a minimum level (INFO < WARN < ERROR). log(level, text) sends [<LEVEL>] <text> to every handler when the level is at least the minimum. Read the minimum level, then n lines LEVEL text (text is one word); register a handler that prints the message and another that counts messages. Print the passing messages as they arrive, then Handled: <count>.

## The idea
A lambda is a short anonymous function and a method reference is an even shorter one. Streams, Optional and the functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) let you describe what to do rather than how to loop.

## Step by step
1. INFO, WARN, ERROR.
2. Define the class Logger:
   - Private final Level min.
   - Private final List<Consumer<String>> handlers = ArrayList<>().
   - Define the function Logger(min):
     - Store min in this.min.
   - Define the function addHandler(h):
     - Run handlers.add(h).
   - Define the function log(level, text):
     - If level.compareTo(min) < 0:
       - Return from the function.
     - FOR Consumer<String> h : handlers.
       - Run h.accept("[" + level + "] " + text).
3. Store Logger(Level.valueOf(the next word read)) in logger.
4. Store all zeros in count.
5. Run logger.addHandler(print).
6. Run logger.addHandler(msg => count[0]++).
7. Read n from the input.
8. Let i go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Run logger.log(Level.valueOf(the next word read), the next word read).
9. Print "Handled: " + count[0].

title: A Publisher-Subscriber Pipeline
statement: Simulate a reactive pipeline: `Publisher<T>` keeps subscribers (`Consumer<T>`); `map(f)` and `filter(p)` return new publishers that pass on only transformed or matching items. Read `n` integers and publish them through `filter(x -> x % 2 == 0)` then `map(x -> x * 10)`; the subscriber prints `Got <value>` for each, and a second subscriber on the source counts all items. After the last item print `Source items: <n>`.
pseudocode:
CLASS Publisher
  private final List<Consumer<T>> subscribers = ArrayList<>()
  FUNCTION subscribe(s)
    CALL subscribers.add(s)
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION publish(item)
    FOR Consumer<T> s : subscribers
      CALL s.accept(item)
    END FOR
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION filter(keep)
    SET next = Publisher<>()
    subscribe(x ... WHERE THE STEPS ARE:
      IF keep.test(x) THEN
        CALL next.publish(x)
      END IF
    RETURN next
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION map(T, f)
    SET next = Publisher<>()
    CALL subscribe(x => next.publish(f.apply(x)))
    RETURN next
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
READ n
SET a = new int[n]
FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ a[i]
END FOR
SET source = Publisher<>()
SET count = all zeros
CALL source.subscribe(x => count[0]++)
CALL source.filter(x => x MOD 2 = 0).map(x => x * 10).subscribe(x => System.out.println("Got " + x))
FOR int x : a
  CALL source.publish(x)
END FOR
PRINT "Source items: " + count[0]

Read n integers and publish them through filter(x -> x % 2 == 0) then map(x -> x * 10); the subscriber prints Got <value> for each, and a second subscriber on the source counts all items. After the last item print Source items: <n>.

A lambda is a short anonymous function and a method reference is an even shorter one. Streams, Optional and the functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) let you describe what to do rather than how to loop.

     - Run subscribers.add(s).
   - Define the function publish(item):
     - FOR Consumer<T> s : subscribers.
       - Run s.accept(item).
   - Define the function filter(keep):
     - Store Publisher<>() in next.
     - Subscribe(x .., where the steps are:
       - If keep.test(x):
         - Run next.publish(x).
     - Give back next.
   - Define the function map(T, f):

     - Run subscribe(x => next.publish(f.apply(x))).
     - Give back next.
2. Read n from the input.
3. Store new int[n] in a.

title: A Mini Query Engine
statement: Build a tiny in-memory table with generics, lambdas and streams: `Table<T>` with `where(Predicate<T>)`, `orderBy(Comparator<T>)`, `limit(int)` and `select(Function<T, R>)`. Read `n` rows `name marks`, then `min` and `k`. Query: rows with marks at least `min`, ordered by marks (highest first, ties by name), the first `k`, selecting `<name>(<marks>)`. Print the selected values one per line (or `No rows`).
pseudocode:
CLASS Row
  FUNCTION Row(name, marks)
    SET this.name = name
    SET this.marks = marks
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS Table
  private final List<T> rows
  FUNCTION Table(rows)
    SET this.rows = rows
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION where(p)
    RETURN Table<>(rows.stream().filter(p).collect(Collectors.toList()))
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION orderBy(c)
    RETURN Table<>(rows.stream().sorted(c).collect(Collectors.toList()))
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION limit(k)
    RETURN Table<>(rows.stream().limit(k).collect(Collectors.toList()))
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION select(T, f)
    RETURN rows.stream().map(f).collect(Collectors.toList())
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
READ n
SET rows = ArrayList<>()
FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
  CALL rows.add(Row(the next word read, the next number read))
END FOR
READ min, k
SET result = Table<>(rows).where(r => r.marks >= min).orderBy((x, y) => x.marks ≠ y.marks ? y.marks - x.marks : x.name.compareTo(y.name)).limit(k).select(r => r.name + "(" + r.marks + ")")
IF result.isEmpty() THEN
  PRINT "No rows"
END IF
FOR String s : result
  PRINT s
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
Build a tiny in-memory table with generics, lambdas and streams: Table<T> with where(Predicate<T>), orderBy(Comparator<T>), limit(int) and select(Function<T, R>). Read n rows name marks, then min and k. Query: rows with marks at least min, ordered by marks (highest first, ties by name), the first k, selecting <name>(<marks>). Print the selected values one per line (or No rows).

## The idea
A lambda is a short anonymous function and a method reference is an even shorter one. Streams, Optional and the functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) let you describe what to do rather than how to loop.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Row:
   - Define the function Row(name, marks):
     - Store name in this.name.
     - Store marks in this.marks.
2. Define the class Table:
   - Private final List<T> rows.
   - Define the function Table(rows):
     - Store rows in this.rows.
   - Define the function where(p):
     - Give back Table<>(rows.stream().filter(p).collect(Collectors.toList())).
   - Define the function orderBy(c):
     - Give back Table<>(rows.stream().sorted(c).collect(Collectors.toList())).
   - Define the function limit(k):
     - Give back Table<>(rows.stream().limit(k).collect(Collectors.toList())).
   - Define the function select(T, f):
     - Give back rows.stream().map(f).collect(Collectors.toList()).
3. Read n from the input.
4. Store ArrayList<>() in rows.
5. Let i go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Run rows.add(Row(the next word read, the next number read)).
6. Read min, k from the input.
7. Store Table<>(rows).where(r => r.marks >= min).orderBy((x, y) => x.marks ≠ y.marks ? y.marks - x.marks : x.name.compareTo(y.name)).limit(k).select(r => r.name + "(" + r.marks + ")") in result.
8. If result.isEmpty():
   - Print "No rows".
9. FOR String s : result.
   - Print s.

title: Dockerfile for a Node.js App
statement:
Containerise a Node.js app:
- start from a **Node 20** image (`node:20...`)
- set the working directory to `/app`
- copy `package*.json` and run `npm install` **before** copying the rest of the code, so Docker can cache the dependencies
- copy the rest of the source
- document port `3000`
- start it with `node server.js` in exec form (`CMD ["node", "server.js"]`)

Write the Dockerfile in the editor. It is checked instruction by instruction; nothing is built or run.

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

title: A Safer Image
statement:
Write a small Dockerfile that follows good practice:
- a **pinned** base image tag (no `latest`), for example `alpine:3.19`
- a working directory
- create a non-root user and switch to it with `USER` (not `root`)
- a `HEALTHCHECK`
- a `CMD`

Write the Dockerfile in the editor. It is checked instruction by instruction; nothing is built or run.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
FROM alpine:3.19
WORKDIR /app
RUN adduser -D appuser
COPY . .
USER appuser
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
CMD ["./start.sh"]

title: A GitHub Actions Workflow
statement:
Write a GitHub Actions workflow:
- named `CI`
- runs on **push** to `main` and on **pull requests** to `main`
- one job called `test` on `ubuntu-latest`
- its steps: check out the code with `actions/checkout@v4`, run `npm ci`, then run `npm test`

Write the YAML in the editor. Its structure is checked; nothing is deployed.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

title: Deploy When a Tag Is Pushed
statement:
Write a GitHub Actions workflow that releases on version tags:
- triggers on **push** of tags that match `v*`
- a job `build` on `ubuntu-latest` that runs `docker build -t app .`
- a job `deploy` that **needs** `build`, on `ubuntu-latest`, and runs `./deploy.sh`

Write the YAML in the editor. Its structure is checked; nothing is deployed.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
name: Release
on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*'
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t app .
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh

title: Docker Compose: Web and Database
statement:
Write a `docker-compose.yml` with two services:
- `web`: built from the current folder (`build: .`), publishes **8080:80**, and `depends_on` `db`
- `db`: image `postgres:16`, environment `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` set to `secret`, and a named volume `dbdata` mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data`

Declare the `dbdata` volume at the top level.

Write the YAML in the editor. Its structure is checked; nothing is deployed.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  dbdata:

title: A Kubernetes Deployment
statement:
Write a Kubernetes **Deployment**:
- `apiVersion: apps/v1`, `kind: Deployment`, named `web`
- **3** replicas
- selects pods labelled `app: web` (`spec.selector.matchLabels`), and the pod template carries the same label
- one container `web` using the image `nginx:1.27` that exposes `containerPort` **80**

Write the YAML in the editor. Its structure is checked; nothing is deployed.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80

title: A Kubernetes Service
statement:
Write a Kubernetes **Service** that exposes the `web` pods inside the cluster:
- `apiVersion: v1`, `kind: Service`, named `web`
- type `ClusterIP`
- selects pods labelled `app: web`
- forwards port **80** to the container's `targetPort` **80**

Write the YAML in the editor. Its structure is checked; nothing is deployed.
outputFormat: The checks pass when it has the parts above.
solution:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

title: Date Sanity Check
statement: A form checks a day, month and year. Month must be 1 to 12; day must fit the month (February has 29 days in a leap year, otherwise 28). Print `Valid` or `Invalid`.
solution:
d, m, y = map(int, input().split())
leap = y % 4 == 0 and (y % 100 != 0 or y % 400 == 0)
days = [31, 29 if leap else 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]
print("Valid" if 1 <= m <= 12 and 1 <= d <= days[m - 1] else "Invalid")
pseudocode:
READ d, m, y
SET leap = y MOD 4 = 0 AND (y MOD 100 ≠ 0 OR y MOD 400 = 0)
SET days = [31, 29 if leap else 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]
PRINT "Valid" if 1 <= m <= 12 AND 1 <= d <= days[m - 1] else "Invalid"
explanation:
## What the program does
A form checks a day, month and year. Month must be 1 to 12; day must fit the month (February has 29 days in a leap year, otherwise 28). Print Valid or Invalid.

## The idea
An if / elif / else ladder runs the first branch whose condition is true. Combine tests with and, or and not, and remember that empty values and zero count as false.

## Step by step
1. Read d, m, y from the input.
2. Store y MOD 4 = 0 AND (y MOD 100 ≠ 0 OR y MOD 400 = 0) in leap.
3. Store [31, 29 if leap else 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31] in days.
4. Print "Valid" if 1 <= m <= 12 AND 1 <= d <= days[m - 1] else "Invalid".

title: Twin Prime Pairs
statement: A maths club lists twin primes (primes that differ by 2) up to `n`. Print each pair as `p q` on its own line, or `None`.
pseudocode:
READ n
FUNCTION prime(x)
  IF x < 2 THEN
    RETURN false
  END IF
  FOR d FROM 2 TO int(x ^ 0.5) + 1 - 1
    IF x MOD d = 0 THEN
      RETURN false
    END IF
  END FOR
  RETURN true
END FUNCTION
SET found = false
FOR p FROM 2 TO n - 1 - 1
  IF prime(p) AND prime(p + 2) AND p + 2 <= n THEN
    PRINT p, p + 2
    SET found = true
  END IF
END FOR
IF NOT found THEN
  PRINT "nothing"
END IF
explanation:
## What the program does
A maths club lists twin primes (primes that differ by 2) up to n. Print each pair as p q on its own line, or None.

A loop repeats steps. Decide what changes each pass and when it must stop, and keep running results in variables that start with a known value.

## Step by step
1. Read n from the input.
2. Define the function prime(x):
   - If x < 2:
     - Give back false.
   - Let d go from 2 up to int(x ^ 0.5) + 1 - 1, and for each value:
     - If x MOD d = 0:
       - Give back false.
   - Give back true.
3. Store false in found.
4. Let p go from 2 up to n - 1 - 1, and for each value:
   - If prime(p) AND prime(p + 2) AND p + 2 <= n:
     - Print p, p + 2.
     - Store true in found.
5. If NOT found:

a = input().split()[1:]
b = input().split()[1:]
a = list(map(int, a))
b = list(map(int, b))
i = j = 0
out = []
while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
    if a[i] <= b[j]:
        out.append(a[i])
        i += 1
    else:
        out.append(b[j])
        j += 1
out += a[i:] + b[j:]
print(*out)
pseudocode:
READ a
READ b
SET a = list(map(int, a))
SET b = list(map(int, b))
SET i = j = 0
SET out = an empty list
WHILE i < len(a) AND j < len(b)
  IF a[i] <= b[j] THEN
    ADD a[i] TO out
    SET i = i + 1
  ELSE
    ADD b[j] TO out
    SET j = j + 1
  END IF
END WHILE
SET out = out + a[i:] + b[j:]
PRINT *out
explanation:
## What the program does
Two sections have sorted roll numbers. Merge them into one sorted list without using sort on the whole list (use two pointers) and print it.

## The idea
A list keeps order and can change, a tuple keeps order but cannot change, and a set keeps only distinct items. Slicing, sorting and the set operations (union, intersection, difference) solve most tasks.

## Step by step
1. Read a from the input.
2. Read b from the input.
3. Store list(map(int, a)) in a.
4. Store list(map(int, b)) in b.
5. Store j = 0 in i.
6. Store an empty list in out.
7. Keep repeating while i < len(a) AND j < len(b):
   - If a[i] <= b[j]:
     - ADD a[i] TO out.
     - Add 1 to i.
   - Otherwise:
     - ADD b[j] TO out.
     - Add 1 to j.
8. Store out + a[i:] + b[j:] in out.
9. Print *out.

title: Closest Pair of Points
statement: A drone sees `n` points as `(x, y)` tuples. Print the squared distance of the closest pair of different points.
pseudocode:
READ n
READ list pts
SET best = nothing
FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
  FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
    SET d = (pts[i][0] - pts[j][0]) ^ 2 + (pts[i][1] - pts[j][1]) ^ 2
    IF best is nothing OR d < best THEN
      SET best = d
    END IF
  END FOR
END FOR
PRINT best

## What the program does

## Step by step
1. Read n from the input.
2. Read list pts from the input.
3. Store nothing in best.
4. Let i go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Let j go from i + 1 up to n - 1, and for each value:
     - Store (pts[i][0] - pts[j][0]) ^ 2 + (pts[i][1] - pts[j][1]) ^ 2 in d.
     - If best is nothing OR d < best:
       - Store d in best.

title: Roman Numeral Translator
statement: Using a dictionary of the symbols I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000, convert a Roman numeral to a number (subtract when a smaller symbol comes before a larger one).
pseudocode:
SET val = {"I": 1, "V": 5, "X": 10, "L": 50, "C": 100, "D": 500, "M": 1000}
READ s
SET total = 0
FOR EACH i, ch IN enumerate(s)
  IF i + 1 < len(s) AND val[ch] < val[s[i + 1]] THEN
    SET total = total - val[ch]
  ELSE
    SET total = total + val[ch]
  END IF
END FOR
PRINT total

title: Bank Transfer Ledger
statement: Accounts start with balances. Then `t` transfers `from to amount` happen; a transfer is skipped if `from` lacks funds. Print the final balances sorted by account.
inputFormat: First line `n t`, then `n` lines `account balance`, then `t` transfers.
pseudocode:
READ n, t
SET b = an empty dictionary
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ a, v
  SET b[a] = int(v)
END FOR
FOR _ FROM 0 TO t - 1
  READ f, to, amt
  SET amt = int(amt)
  IF b[f] >= amt THEN
    SET b[f] = b[f] - amt
    SET b[to] = b[to] + amt
  END IF
END FOR
FOR EACH a IN sorted(b)
  PRINT a, b[a]
END FOR

## What the program does
Accounts start with balances. Then t transfers from to amount happen; a transfer is skipped if from lacks funds. Print the final balances sorted by account.

A dictionary maps keys to values and finds a value by its key in about one step. Use get() for a safe lookup, setdefault() or a counter to group and count, and nested dictionaries for tables.

## Step by step
1. Read n, t from the input.
2. Store an empty dictionary in b.
3. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read a, v from the input.
   - Store int(v) in b[a].
4. Let _ go from 0 up to t - 1, and for each value:
   - Read f, to, amt from the input.
   - Store int(amt) in amt.
   - If b[f] >= amt:
     - Store b[f] - amt in b[f].
     - Store b[to] + amt in b[to].
5. Go through every a in sorted(b), and for each one:
   - Print a, b[a].

title: Isomorphic Words
statement: Two words are isomorphic if letters of the first can be replaced one-to-one to give the second. Print `Yes` or `No` (same length required).
pseudocode:
READ a
READ b
IF len(a) ≠ len(b) THEN
  PRINT "No"
ELSE
  SET m, used, ok = {}, set(), true
  FOR EACH x, y IN zip(a, b)
    IF x in m THEN
      IF m[x] ≠ y THEN
        SET ok = false
      END IF
    ELSE IF y in used THEN
      SET ok = false
    ELSE
      SET m[x] = y
      CALL used.add(y)
    END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT "Yes" if ok else "No"
END IF
explanation:
## What the program does
Two words are isomorphic if letters of the first can be replaced one-to-one to give the second. Print Yes or No (same length required).

## The idea
A dictionary maps keys to values and finds a value by its key in about one step. Use get() for a safe lookup, setdefault() or a counter to group and count, and nested dictionaries for tables.

## Step by step
1. Read a from the input.
2. Read b from the input.
3. If len(a) ≠ len(b):
   - Print "No".
4. Otherwise:
   - Store {}, set(), true in m, used, ok.
   - Go through every x, y in zip(a, b), and for each one:
     - If x in m:
       - If m[x] ≠ y:
         - Store false in ok.
     - Otherwise, if y in used:
       - Store false in ok.
     - Otherwise:
       - Store y in m[x].
       - Run used.add(y).
   - Print "Yes" if ok else "No".

title: Employee ID Lookup With Validation
statement: Employees are stored as `id -> name`. Process `q` queries; for an id that exists print the name, for a missing one print `Unknown id <id>`, and if the id is not all digits print `Bad id`.
inputFormat: First line `n q`, then `n` lines `id name`, then `q` queries.
pseudocode:
READ n, q
SET d = an empty dictionary
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ i, name
  SET d[i] = name
END FOR
FOR _ FROM 0 TO q - 1
  READ x
  IF NOT x.isdigit() THEN
    PRINT "Bad id"
  ELSE IF x in d THEN
    PRINT d[x]
  ELSE
    PRINT "Unknown id", x
  END IF
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
Employees are stored as id -> name. Process q queries; for an id that exists print the name, for a missing one print Unknown id <id>, and if the id is not all digits print Bad id.

## The idea
A dictionary maps keys to values and finds a value by its key in about one step. Use get() for a safe lookup, setdefault() or a counter to group and count, and nested dictionaries for tables.

## Step by step
1. Read n, q from the input.
2. Store an empty dictionary in d.
3. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read i, name from the input.
   - Store name in d[i].
4. Let _ go from 0 up to q - 1, and for each value:
   - Read x from the input.
   - If NOT x.isdigit():
     - Print "Bad id".
   - Otherwise, if x in d:
     - Print d[x].
   - Otherwise:
     - Print "Unknown id", x.

END FOR
explanation:

A drone sorts waypoints x y by distance from the origin (nearest first; ties by x then y). Print the points one per line.

## The idea

statement: A flaky service fails the first `f` times it is called and then succeeds. A decorator `retry(times)` calls the function up to `times` times and returns `success after k tries` or `failed`. Read `f times` and print the result.

  END FUNCTION
  RETURN deco

title: Class Decorator Counter
statement: A class decorator `track` gives a class a counter of how many objects were created. After creating `n` objects of `Ticket` print `created n`.
pseudocode:
FUNCTION track(cls)
  SET cls.count = 0
  SET original = cls.__init__
  FUNCTION init(self, *a)
    SET cls.count = cls.count + 1
    CALL original(self, *a)
  END FUNCTION
  SET cls.__init__ = init
  RETURN cls
END FUNCTION
@track
CLASS Ticket
  FUNCTION __init__(self, no)
    SET self.no = no
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
FOR i FROM 0 TO the number read - 1
  CALL Ticket(i)
END FOR
PRINT "created {Ticket.count}"
explanation:
## What the program does
A class decorator track gives a class a counter of how many objects were created. After creating n objects of Ticket print created n.

## The idea
A function packs a task under a name so it can be reused. It receives parameters, does its work and gives back one value with return.

## Step by step
1. Define the function track(cls):
   - Store 0 in cls.count.
   - Store cls.__init__ in original.
   - Define the function init(self, *a):
     - Add 1 to cls.count.
     - Run original(self, *a).
   - Store init in cls.__init__.
   - Give back cls.
2. @track.
3. Define the class Ticket:
   - Define the function __init__(self, no):
     - Store no in self.no.
4. Let i go from 0 up to the number read - 1, and for each value:
   - Run Ticket(i).
5. Print "created {Ticket.count}".

the program prints:

title: Playlist Object
statement: A `Playlist` stores song titles with `add(title)`, `remove(title)` and `show()`. Commands: `add t`, `remove t`, `show`. `show` prints the songs joined by ` | ` or `(empty)`.

CLASS Playlist
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.songs = an empty list
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION add(self, t)
    ADD t TO self.songs
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION remove(self, t)
    IF t in self.songs THEN
      CALL self.songs.remove(t)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

statement: A `Wallet` allows spending at most `limit` per day. `spend(x)` returns `Spent` when the total for the day stays within the limit, else `Limit exceeded`; `new_day()` clears the day's total. Process commands.

title: Super Init Chain
statement: A `Person` stores a name; `Student` extends it with a roll number using `super().__init__`, and `Prefect` extends `Student` with a duty. Each line `name roll duty`; print `Prefect <name> (<roll>) on <duty>`.

  FUNCTION __init__(self, name)
    SET self.name = name

CLASS Student EXTENDS Person
  FUNCTION __init__(self, name, roll)
    CALL super().__init__(name)
    SET self.roll = roll
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS Prefect EXTENDS Student
  FUNCTION __init__(self, name, roll, duty)
    CALL super().__init__(name, roll)
    SET self.duty = duty
  END FUNCTION

    RETURN f"Prefect {self.name} ({self.roll}) on {self.duty}"
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS

   - Define the function __init__(self, name):
     - Store name in self.name.
2. Define the class Student EXTENDS Person:

     - Run super().__init__(name).

statement: `Point(x, y)` compares equal to another `Point` with the same coordinates. `Point3D(x, y, z)` extends it and also needs `z` to match. For each line `kind x y [z] kind x y [z]` print whether the two objects are equal (`True` or `False`).

    ...

CLASS Rect EXTENDS Shape

    SET self.l, self.w = l, w

title: Abstract Storage Backends
statement: An abstract `Storage` declares `save(key, value)` and `load(key)`. `MemoryStorage` keeps values in a dictionary; `LoggingStorage` does the same and also counts saves. Commands: `save k v`, `load k`, `saves` (for the logging one only). Use `LoggingStorage` and print `load` results (or `missing`) and the save count.
pseudocode:
CLASS Storage EXTENDS ABC
  @abstractmethod
  FUNCTION save(self, k, v)
    ...
  END FUNCTION
  @abstractmethod
  FUNCTION load(self, k)
    ...
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS MemoryStorage EXTENDS Storage
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.d = an empty dictionary
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION save(self, k, v)
    SET self.d[k] = v
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION load(self, k)
    RETURN self.d.get(k, "missing")
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS LoggingStorage EXTENDS MemoryStorage
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    CALL super().__init__()
    SET self.count = 0
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION save(self, k, v)
    SET self.count = self.count + 1
    CALL super().save(k, v)
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
SET s = LoggingStorage()
READ n
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ c
  IF c[0] = "save" THEN
    CALL s.save(c[1], c[2])
  ELSE IF c[0] = "load" THEN
    PRINT s.load(c[1])
  ELSE
    PRINT s.count
  END IF
END FOR

A class bundles data (attributes) with the methods that work on it. Encapsulation hides internals behind methods and properties, inheritance reuses a parent class, abstraction fixes the shape of subclasses, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object.

title: Iterable Countdown Class
statement: A `Countdown(n)` class is iterable: it yields `n, n-1, ..., 1` through `__iter__` and `__next__`. Print the numbers separated by spaces, then the total of the numbers.
pseudocode:
CLASS Countdown
  FUNCTION __init__(self, n)
    SET self.n = n
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION __iter__(self)
    RETURN self
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION __next__(self)
    IF self.n <= 0 THEN
      raise StopIteration
    END IF
    SET v = self.n
    SET self.n = self.n - 1
    RETURN v
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
READ list vals
PRINT *vals
PRINT sum(vals)
explanation:
## What the program does
A Countdown(n) class is iterable: it yields n, n-1, ..., 1 through __iter__ and __next__. Print the numbers separated by spaces, then the total of the numbers.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Countdown:
   - Define the function __init__(self, n):
     - Store n in self.n.
   - Define the function __iter__(self):
     - Give back self.
   - Define the function __next__(self):
     - If self.n <= 0:
       - Raise StopIteration.
     - Store self.n in v.
     - Store self.n - 1 in self.n.
     - Give back v.

title: Car With Engine Part
statement: A `Car` has an `Engine` part. `Engine.start()` uses 1 litre and returns whether the tank had fuel; the `Car` has `drive(km)` which uses `km // 10` litres if enough fuel is present (else it says `Out of fuel` and keeps the fuel). Commands: `fuel x`, `drive km`. Print the result of each `drive` (`Driven` or `Out of fuel`) and the fuel left after it.
pseudocode:
CLASS Engine
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.fuel = 0
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION use(self, litres)
    IF litres > self.fuel THEN
      RETURN false
    END IF
    SET self.fuel = self.fuel - litres
    RETURN true
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS Car
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.engine = Engine()
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION drive(self, km)
    RETURN "Driven" if self.engine.use(km DIV 10) else "Out of fuel"
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
SET car = Car()
READ n
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ c, x
  IF c = "fuel" THEN
    SET car.engine.fuel = car.engine.fuel + int(x)
  ELSE
    PRINT car.drive(int(x)), car.engine.fuel
  END IF
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
A Car has an Engine part. Engine.start() uses 1 litre and returns whether the tank had fuel; the Car has drive(km) which uses km // 10 litres if enough fuel is present (else it says Out of fuel and keeps the fuel). Commands: fuel x, drive km. Print the result of each drive (Driven or Out of fuel) and the fuel left after it.

## The idea
A class bundles data (attributes) with the methods that work on it. Encapsulation hides internals behind methods and properties, inheritance reuses a parent class, abstraction fixes the shape of subclasses, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Engine:
   - Define the function __init__(self):
     - Store 0 in self.fuel.
   - Define the function use(self, litres):
     - If litres > self.fuel:
       - Give back false.
     - Store self.fuel - litres in self.fuel.
     - Give back true.
2. Define the class Car:
   - Define the function __init__(self):
     - Store Engine() in self.engine.
   - Define the function drive(self, km):
     - Give back "Driven" if self.engine.use(km DIV 10) else "Out of fuel".
3. Store Car() in car.
4. Read n from the input.
5. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read c, x from the input.
   - If c = "fuel":
     - Store car.engine.fuel + int(x) in car.engine.fuel.
   - Otherwise:
     - Print car.drive(int(x)), car.engine.fuel.

title: Shopping Cart Composition
statement: A `Cart` holds `Product` objects with a price. `add name price`, `remove name` (removes the first product with that name, ignoring missing ones), and `total` (print the sum). Process the commands.
pseudocode:
CLASS Product
  FUNCTION __init__(self, name, price)
    SET self.name, self.price = name, price
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS Cart
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.items = an empty list
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION add(self, n, p)
    ADD Product(n, p) TO self.items
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION remove(self, n)
    FOR EACH i, p IN enumerate(self.items)
      IF p.name = n THEN
        del self.items[i]
        RETURN
      END IF
    END FOR
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION total(self)
    RETURN sum(p.price for p in self.items)
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
SET c = Cart()
READ n
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ x
  IF x[0] = "add" THEN
    CALL c.add(x[1], int(x[2]))
  ELSE IF x[0] = "remove" THEN
    CALL c.remove(x[1])
  ELSE
    PRINT c.total()
  END IF
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
A Cart holds Product objects with a price. add name price, remove name (removes the first product with that name, ignoring missing ones), and total (print the sum). Process the commands.

## The idea
A class bundles data (attributes) with the methods that work on it. Encapsulation hides internals behind methods and properties, inheritance reuses a parent class, abstraction fixes the shape of subclasses, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Product:
   - Define the function __init__(self, name, price):
     - Store name, price in self.name, self.price.
2. Define the class Cart:
   - Define the function __init__(self):
     - Store an empty list in self.items.
   - Define the function add(self, n, p):
     - ADD Product(n, p) TO self.items.
   - Define the function remove(self, n):
     - Go through every i, p in enumerate(self.items), and for each one:
       - If p.name = n:
         - Del self.items[i].
         - Return from the function.
   - Define the function total(self):
     - Give back sum(p.price for p in self.items).
3. Store Cart() in c.
4. Read n from the input.
5. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read x from the input.
   - If x[0] = "add":
     - Run c.add(x[1], int(x[2])).
   - Otherwise, if x[0] = "remove":
     - Run c.remove(x[1]).
   - Otherwise:
     - Print c.total().

title: Class Registry With Decorator
statement: A `Registry` class keeps a dictionary of handlers; `Registry.register(name)` is a decorator that stores a function. Handlers `double` and `negate` are registered. Each line `name x`; print the handler's result or `unknown`.
pseudocode:
CLASS Registry
  SET handlers = an empty dictionary
  @classmethod
  FUNCTION register(cls, name)
    FUNCTION deco(fn)
      SET cls.handlers[name] = fn
      RETURN fn
    END FUNCTION
    RETURN deco
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
@Registry.register("double")
FUNCTION double(x)
  RETURN x * 2
END FUNCTION
@Registry.register("negate")
FUNCTION negate(x)
  RETURN -x
END FUNCTION
READ n
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ a, x
  SET f = Registry.handlers.get(a)
  PRINT f(int(x)) if f else "unknown"
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
A Registry class keeps a dictionary of handlers; Registry.register(name) is a decorator that stores a function. Handlers double and negate are registered. Each line name x; print the handler's result or unknown.

## The idea
A class bundles data (attributes) with the methods that work on it. Encapsulation hides internals behind methods and properties, inheritance reuses a parent class, abstraction fixes the shape of subclasses, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Registry:
   - Store an empty dictionary in handlers.
   - @classmethod.
   - Define the function register(cls, name):
     - Define the function deco(fn):
       - Store fn in cls.handlers[name].
       - Give back fn.
     - Give back deco.
2. @Registry.register("double").
3. Define the function double(x):
   - Give back x * 2.
4. @Registry.register("negate").
5. Define the function negate(x):
   - Give back -x.
6. Read n from the input.
7. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read a, x from the input.
   - Store Registry.handlers.get(a) in f.
   - Print f(int(x)) if f else "unknown".

double -8

the program prints:

-16

title: Parking Lot Objects
statement: A `ParkingLot` with `cap` slots holds `Car` objects. `park plate` parks a car if there is room (`Parked` or `Full`); `leave plate` removes it (`Left` or `Not here`); `free` prints the free slots. Print each response.
pseudocode:
CLASS Car
  FUNCTION __init__(self, plate)
    SET self.plate = plate
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS ParkingLot
  FUNCTION __init__(self, cap)
    SET self.cap = cap
    SET self.cars = an empty list
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION park(self, plate)
    IF len(self.cars) >= self.cap THEN
      RETURN "Full"
    END IF
    ADD Car(plate) TO self.cars
    RETURN "Parked"
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION leave(self, plate)
    FOR EACH c IN self.cars
      IF c.plate = plate THEN
        CALL self.cars.remove(c)
        RETURN "Left"
      END IF
    END FOR
    RETURN "Not here"
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION free(self)
    RETURN self.cap - len(self.cars)
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
READ cap, n
SET lot = ParkingLot(cap)
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ c
  IF c[0] = "park" THEN
    PRINT lot.park(c[1])
  ELSE IF c[0] = "leave" THEN
    PRINT lot.leave(c[1])
  ELSE
    PRINT lot.free()
  END IF
END FOR
explanation:
## What the program does
A ParkingLot with cap slots holds Car objects. park plate parks a car if there is room (Parked or Full); leave plate removes it (Left or Not here); free prints the free slots. Print each response.

## The idea
A class bundles data (attributes) with the methods that work on it. Encapsulation hides internals behind methods and properties, inheritance reuses a parent class, abstraction fixes the shape of subclasses, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object.

## Step by step
1. Define the class Car:
   - Define the function __init__(self, plate):
     - Store plate in self.plate.
2. Define the class ParkingLot:
   - Define the function __init__(self, cap):
     - Store cap in self.cap.
     - Store an empty list in self.cars.
   - Define the function park(self, plate):
     - If len(self.cars) >= self.cap:
       - Give back "Full".
     - ADD Car(plate) TO self.cars.
     - Give back "Parked".
   - Define the function leave(self, plate):
     - Go through every c in self.cars, and for each one:
       - If c.plate = plate:
         - Run self.cars.remove(c).
         - Give back "Left".
     - Give back "Not here".
   - Define the function free(self):
     - Give back self.cap - len(self.cars).
3. Read cap, n from the input.
4. Store ParkingLot(cap) in lot.
5. Let _ go from 0 up to n - 1, and for each value:
   - Read c from the input.
   - If c[0] = "park":
     - Print lot.park(c[1]).
   - Otherwise, if c[0] = "leave":
     - Print lot.leave(c[1]).
   - Otherwise:
     - Print lot.free().

title: Employee Directory Class
statement: An `EmployeeDirectory` keeps `Employee` objects by id. `add id name dept`, `find id` (prints `name (dept)` or `not found`) and `count dept` (prints how many employees are in the department). Process the commands.
pseudocode:
CLASS Employee
  FUNCTION __init__(self, i, name, dept)
    SET self.i, self.name, self.dept = i, name, dept
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
CLASS EmployeeDirectory
  FUNCTION __init__(self)
    SET self.by_id = an empty dictionary
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION add(self, i, name, dept)
    SET self.by_id[i] = Employee(i, name, dept)
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION find(self, i)
    SET e = self.by_id.get(i)
    RETURN f"{e.name} ({e.dept})" if e else "NOT found"
  END FUNCTION
  FUNCTION count(self, dept)
    RETURN sum(1 for e in self.by_id.values() if e.dept = dept)
  END FUNCTION
END CLASS
SET d = EmployeeDirectory()
READ n
FOR _ FROM 0 TO n - 1
  READ c
  IF c[0] = "add" THEN
    CALL d.add(c[1], c[2], c[3])
  ELSE IF c[0] = "find" THEN
    PRINT d.find(c[1])
  ELSE
    PRINT d.count(c[1])
  END IF
END FOR
